Aspect:
Punctuation

Standalone punctuation is stripped from name and text search terms.
Applies to LUX field index patterns: Keyword; Exact Match; sometimes Field Range Index support depending on collation/value query usage
Default / index-only behavior: Punctuation and space tokens are not generally indexed as words in the universal index; word queries involving punctuation do not use punctuation in index resolution.
How false positives / negatives arise: A punctuation-sensitive search can select candidates that contain the word tokens but not the same punctuation relationship. If such a query is negated, false positives in A can become false negatives in NOT A.
LUX customer example / relevance: Names, identifiers, product codes, military-style codes, and collection terms such as “O’Keeffe”, “AT&T”, or “F-12”.
Behavior change / mitigation: For exact values, prefer exact value queries, string field range equality with an appropriate collation such as codepoint, or isolated/tagged fields for exact identifiers. For Optic, filter candidate documents with cts.contains when exact punctuation semantics matter.
Recommended LUX stance: Do not promise exact punctuation semantics from Keyword fields alone. Route exact identifiers/names through Exact Match or range-backed fields when possible; otherwise conditionally filter.
Optic implication: Use op.fromSearchDocs(candidateCtsQuery) to constrain candidates, then add cts.contains(doc, exactCtsQuery) via op.call when the index cannot prove the punctuation-sensitive match.
Sources: Bob Starbird Unfiltered Searches; MarkLogic cts:search docs; Optic docs; Teams discussion

Applies to LUX field index patterns: Keyword; Exact Match; sometimes Field Range Index support depending on collation/value query usage
Default / index-only behavior: Whitespace tokens are not generally indexed as words in the universal index; whitespace-sensitive word/value behavior is not always provable from token indexes.
How false positives / negatives arise: Indexes may prove the component tokens exist but not the exact whitespace form. NOT of such a query can under-select when index resolution is approximate.
LUX customer example / relevance: Multi-word names/titles where “New York”, “New  York”, and joined/normalized variants are user-visible distinctions.
Behavior change / mitigation: Use exact value semantics or field/range indexes with suitable collation for exact-match fields. Filter with cts.contains when whitespace sensitivity is part of user intent.
Recommended LUX stance: Keyword should remain recall-oriented. Exact Match should carry stricter semantics; filter only for user-facing searches that require exact whitespace behavior.
Optic implication: Parameterize or build the CTS query with whitespace-sensitive options for the filter step; keep candidate query as selective as safely possible.
Sources: Bob Starbird Unfiltered Searches; MarkLogic cts:search docs; Optic docs

Default / index-only behavior: Case-insensitive queries can be resolved from the index; case-sensitive searches require the right index support for index-only accuracy. Bob’s notes call out lower-case case-sensitive searches as a source of inaccurate unfiltered results.
How false positives / negatives arise: A case-sensitive query can select candidates based on case-insensitive terms, especially when fast case-sensitive searches are not available for the scenario.
LUX customer example / relevance: Names, acronyms, and identifiers where “US”, “us”, “May”, and “may” should not be interchangeable.
Behavior change / mitigation: Enable fast case-sensitive searches where case-sensitive search is important; use exact value/range-backed fields for exact identifiers; otherwise filter.
Recommended LUX stance: Default Keyword fields should stay forgiving unless the UI explicitly offers case-sensitive behavior. Exact-match fields should be tested for exact case expectations.
Optic implication: Do not rely on op.fromSearch/op.fromSearchDocs alone for CTS filtered behavior; add cts.contains on doc when case-sensitive exactness matters.
Sources: Bob Starbird Unfiltered Searches; MarkLogic cts:search docs; Teams discussion

Default / index-only behavior: Diacritic-insensitive behavior is index-friendly; diacritic-sensitive searches may need fast diacritic-sensitive searches for better index resolution.
How false positives / negatives arise: Without diacritic-sensitive index support, a diacritic-sensitive query can select accent-insensitive candidates that filtering would later reject.
LUX customer example / relevance: Artist/person/place names such as “résumé/resume” style distinctions, European names, and transliteration-sensitive catalog data.
Behavior change / mitigation: Enable fast diacritic-sensitive searches where required; use exact value/range-backed fields for exact strings; filter when diacritic-sensitive precision matters.
Recommended LUX stance: For general Keyword search, diacritic-insensitive behavior is usually desirable for recall. For authoritative identifiers/names, use Exact Match or filter.
Optic implication: Only conditionally filter searches where the UI/query semantics require diacritic-sensitive precision.
Sources: Bob Starbird Unfiltered Searches; MarkLogic cts:search docs

Applies to LUX field index patterns: Keyword primarily; Exact Match should generally avoid stemming
Default / index-only behavior: Stemming broadens term matching. Bob’s notes distinguish word-query and value-query stemming behavior and note that wildcard queries use unstemmed words.
How false positives / negatives arise: Stemmed resolution can admit morphologically related terms that may not satisfy a stricter user expectation. Conversely, stemming implementation details can affect which forms match.
LUX customer example / relevance: User keyword searches across object/person/place text where recall is desired; less appropriate for exact names, codes, and identifiers.
Behavior change / mitigation: Use unstemmed/exact options for exact-match use cases; separate Keyword versus Exact Match field patterns; avoid stemming on exact identifier fields.
Recommended LUX stance: Treat stemming as a recall feature, not a precision guarantee. Do not use Keyword semantics to answer exact-match requirements.
Optic implication: If a stemmed candidate query is used for performance/relevance but exact semantics are required, filter with an unstemmed/exact CTS query.

Applies to LUX field index patterns: Keyword primarily; sometimes Exact Match only if explicitly supported
Default / index-only behavior: MarkLogic supports wildcard search with wildcard-related indexes, but Bob’s notes say problem wildcard queries are still possible with any combination of indexes.
How false positives / negatives arise: Wildcard expansion can over-select candidates. Arbitrary wildcard patterns are not guaranteed to be accurately resolvable unfiltered in the general case.
LUX customer example / relevance: Advanced search terms with prefix/suffix/infix wildcards, partial names, and unknown spellings.
Behavior change / mitigation: Use trailing wildcard indexes, three-character indexes, wildcard word positions, and/or lexicons as appropriate; constrain allowed wildcard patterns; filter high-risk patterns.
Recommended LUX stance: Allow wildcarding as a recall-oriented feature, but identify patterns that require filtering or are too expensive/risky for production defaults.
Optic implication: Push the safest selective wildcard-compatible CTS query into fromSearchDocs; use cts.contains for final correctness when wildcard pattern semantics matter.
Sources: Bob Starbird Unfiltered Searches; MarkLogic cts:search docs

Default / index-only behavior: Phrase accuracy depends on position/phrase-related indexes. Checked searches eliminate phrase false positives during CTS search index resolution; unchecked searches can produce false positives.
How false positives / negatives arise: Without sufficient positions, indexes may know all phrase words exist but not that they occur together in order/proximity.
LUX customer example / relevance: Quoted user searches for names/titles such as “Walter Bradford Cannon” or titles/labels where term adjacency matters.
Behavior change / mitigation: Enable word positions, element/field word positions, and phrase-related index options where phrase search accuracy/performance matters; filter when index evidence is insufficient.
Recommended LUX stance: Quoted phrases are a prime trigger for conditional filtering unless the relevant field pattern is known to have sufficient phrase/position support.
Optic implication: Use candidate phrase/field query in fromSearchDocs when available, then cts.contains(doc, fullPhraseQuery) for customer-visible correctness.
Sources: Bob Starbird Unfiltered Searches; MarkLogic cts:search docs; Optic docs

Default / index-only behavior: Near/proximity queries depend on word positions. MarkLogic examples show near queries can express proximity in Optic via CTS queries, while Optic searches themselves are unfiltered.
How false positives / negatives arise: Indexes may identify both terms without being able to fully prove the requested proximity if positional support is insufficient or not checked.
LUX customer example / relevance: Advanced searches that require one name/title/concept near another.
Behavior change / mitigation: Enable/check positional indexes and use checked CTS behavior; filter in Optic when exact proximity semantics matter.
Recommended LUX stance: Treat proximity as higher-risk than simple term existence. Filter if the field pattern does not explicitly support accurate proximity resolution.
Optic implication: Candidate query should include cheap/selective constraints; cts.contains should contain the exact near/proximity CTS query.
Sources: MarkLogic cts:search docs; Optic search capabilities docs; Bob Starbird Unfiltered Searches

Applies to LUX field index patterns: Keyword field queries; fields over JSON-LD paths; nested content
Default / index-only behavior: Fast element/field word indexes can track field/element names with words, but may not prove phrase/instance relationships without more granular indexes.
How false positives / negatives arise: A fragment can contain the field and the word, or contain parent/child relationships, without the matching term being in the intended same field/subtree instance.
LUX customer example / relevance: JSON-LD documents reuse property names in multiple contexts; path-based fields and broad “AnyText” fields can over-select.
Behavior change / mitigation: Use narrower fields, exact-match fields, range indexes, or TDE/view columns where possible; filter for same-field/same-subtree correctness.
Recommended LUX stance: Be explicit that “field hit” can be candidate-level unless field design/indexes prove the intended scope. Tests should include terms both inside and outside the field path.
Optic implication: For Optic migration, fromSearchDocs can produce candidate docs; cts.contains against doc is the filter equivalent for scoped field semantics.
Sources: Bob Starbird Unfiltered Searches; Teams discussion

Aspect: Field range indexes / structured exact values
Applies to LUX field index patterns: Exact Match; Exclusive Support of Field Range Indexes
Default / index-only behavior: Field range indexes track values appearing in a field and accelerate comparison queries; collation and scalar type define comparison behavior.
How false positives / negatives arise: Range queries are generally stronger for exact structured constraints, but invalid-values settings and collation choices can affect behavior and query-time errors/omissions.
LUX customer example / relevance: Dates, dimensions, sort names, data type filters, identifiers, and fields created specifically for equality/range comparison.
Behavior change / mitigation: Choose scalar type/collation deliberately; prefer codepoint/exact collation for exact string equality; use invalid-values=reject unless a documented reason exists to ignore/skip invalids.
Recommended LUX stance: For customer-facing exact-match promises, prefer range-backed Exact Match / Exclusive Range patterns over broad Keyword fields.
Optic implication: Where an Optic plan can use fromView/fromLexicons/range-backed columns, prefer that over document filtering. Use cts.contains only for residual full-text semantics not represented in rows/indexes.
Sources: MarkLogic field range index docs; Teams discussion

Applies to LUX field index patterns: Exact Match; Exclusive Support of Field Range Indexes
Default / index-only behavior: Field range indexes have invalid-values settings. Bob’s notes call out invalid values and empty scalar values as sources of false positives for unfiltered range queries when invalid values are ignored.
How false positives / negatives arise: If invalid values are ignored/skipped, documents can exist whose content cannot be represented in the range index, affecting range query/lexicon behavior and possibly filtering expectations.
LUX customer example / relevance: Date/dimension fields where source data can be partial, malformed, empty, or not coercible to the intended scalar type.
Behavior change / mitigation: Prefer reject for fields that must support reliable range/equality semantics; otherwise document the consequence of ignore/skip and test query behavior for empty/malformed values.
Recommended LUX stance: For Exclusive Range fields, invalid-values policy is part of the correctness contract and should be reviewed with sample bad data.
Optic implication: If Optic relies on range-index columns, filtering cannot recover values that were not indexed as valid typed values; fix modeling/index policy rather than relying only on post-filtering.
Sources: Bob Starbird Unfiltered Searches; MarkLogic field range index docs

Default / index-only behavior: Bob’s core warning: if A produces false positives in index resolution, then NOT A can produce false negatives.
How false positives / negatives arise: Approximate positive matching is tolerable when filtered later; approximate negation can exclude documents that should remain because the index thought A might match.
LUX customer example / relevance: Advanced search exclusions, boolean NOT, “must not contain”, or negative filters against broad text fields.
Behavior change / mitigation: Avoid applying NOT around query components that are not index-resolvable unless a filtered evaluation is used; rewrite to positive structured constraints where possible.
Recommended LUX stance: NOT is the highest-priority trigger for conditional filtering. If a NOT child can be approximate, require a correctness review/test.
Optic implication: For Optic in ML 12.0.x, place safe positive constraints in fromSearchDocs and apply full Boolean semantics, including NOT, in cts.contains. Be careful with using the exact same approximate NOT query only as candidate selection because it may already have removed true matches.
Sources: Bob Starbird Unfiltered Searches; MarkLogic cts:search docs

Default / index-only behavior: MarkLogic Optic documentation states Optic searches are unfiltered; op.fromSearch selects fragments in the same manner as unfiltered cts:search operations; op.fromSearchDocs is a convenience wrapper around op.fromSearch plus doc/URI join.
How false positives / negatives arise: Any CTS query whose correctness depended on filtered cts:search can return candidate documents in Optic unless an explicit filter is added.
LUX customer example / relevance: Migration from existing CTS search implementation to Optic while preserving customer-visible search result semantics.
Behavior change / mitigation: Use fromSearchDocs/fromSearch for candidate selection and add cts.contains(doc, fullQuery) when filtered CTS semantics are required. Prefer range/view/lexicon accessors for structured patterns where they fully represent the semantics.
Recommended LUX stance: Make filtering conditional and query-shape driven, not global. Start with quotes/phrases, punctuation/whitespace/case/diacritic-sensitive exactness, wildcard edge cases, scoped fields, and NOT.
Optic implication: In ML 12.0.1/12.0.2, this appears to remain the best grounded pattern found in docs and Teams: constrain in fromSearchDocs, filter remaining/full query with cts.contains via op.call.
Confidence: High for 12.0.x; Medium for future 12.1 details
Sources: MarkLogic Optic docs; cts:search docs; Teams discussion; MarkLogic 12 release notes

Applies to LUX field index patterns: Optic migration and query builder implementation
Default / index-only behavior: Current public 12.0 docs show op.fromSearch/op.fromSearchDocs take CTS query objects; internal Teams discussion says parameterized CTS queries and fromDocs were expected for 12.1 but not promised to customers.
How false positives / negatives arise: Parameterization itself does not eliminate false positives; it affects how safely/flexibly query values can be supplied to an Optic plan. Filtering is still about whether results are verified against content.
LUX customer example / relevance: Avoiding eval/string-built CTS queries and enabling reusable Optic plans with customer-provided search parameters.
Behavior change / mitigation: When available, use parameterized CTS query support to improve safety/reuse; still decide separately whether the parameterized query is candidate-only or final filtering logic.
Recommended LUX stance: Describe 12.1 parameterization as overlapping implementation plumbing, not a replacement for filtering, unless release docs explicitly state filtered Optic semantics changed.
Optic implication: Parameterization can make the fromSearchDocs + cts.contains pattern cleaner, but it does not by itself prove index-only correctness.
Sources: Teams discussion; MarkLogic 12.0 release notes; Optic docs
